posts.facebook: What does LeadsLeap's Traffic Co-op actually count? Its help pages say a visitor has to surf your unique Co-op link for at least five seconds. I explain how the exchange works, what credits and cash mean, and why auto-surf bots are not a safe shortcut.
posts.threads: A traffic-exchange link is not the same as a qualified visit. LeadsLeap says Co-op visitors need to surf the link for 5+ seconds. Here's a plain-English guide to the rules, credits, cash and automation limits.
posts.x: LeadsLeap Co-op visits require 5+ seconds of real surfing, according to its tutorial. Here's what counts—and what doesn't:

posts.facebook: LeadsLeap's Co-op is a reciprocal traffic network: you promote your link and may receive traffic back. The key is sending visitors who understand the page and choose to explore it. This guide explains the mechanics and limits.
posts.threads: LeadsLeap Traffic Co-op is a reciprocal traffic network—not a magic source of buyers. Send relevant people, explain the destination, and measure qualifying visits rather than raw clicks.
posts.x: LeadsLeap's Co-op is a reciprocal traffic network, not guaranteed buyers. Understand the qualifying-visit rule before promoting it:

posts.threads: Credits are not cash. LeadsLeap has separate Co-op, PPC, affiliate and credit-encashment mechanisms. Track each category separately so a points balance doesn't get mistaken for withdrawable income.

posts.facebook: LeadsLeap's Daily Active Bonus has a personal activity condition: its current tutorial says members must personally view at least ten ads in a day. Co-op traffic does not replace that personal requirement.
posts.threads: Important detail: LeadsLeap says its Daily Active Bonus requires at least 10 ads viewed personally. Co-op visits and PPC clicks are not counted as your personal ad views.

posts.facebook: PPC and Traffic Co-op are different. LeadsLeap says PPC income comes when a visitor voluntarily clicks an Ad Widget and surfs the advertised site. A page view alone is not a PPC click.
posts.threads: PPC is not the same as Co-op. LeadsLeap says PPC income depends on a visitor voluntarily clicking an Ad Widget and surfing the advertiser's site.

posts.facebook: Before promoting any traffic platform, read its automation policy. LeadsLeap prohibits bots, scripts and macros that simulate human activity on its platform. Our guide focuses on genuine visitors and compliant promotion.
posts.threads: Don't risk an account for automated surfing. LeadsLeap explicitly prohibits bots, scripts and macros that simulate human activity on its platform. Legitimate content promotion is a different activity.
posts.x: LeadsLeap prohibits bots/scripts that simulate human activity on its platform. Promote content; don't automate its surfing:

posts.facebook: A thousand page loads are not necessarily a thousand qualifying Co-op visits. LeadsLeap says it evaluates real surfing duration and traffic quality. Measure qualified visits and actual credits/cash, not just clicks.
posts.threads: Raw clicks can be misleading. For LeadsLeap Co-op, measure visits that meet the surfing rule and compare them with the actual cash and credits recorded in your account.

posts.facebook: If you're testing LeadsLeap, start small: promote a clear guide to a relevant audience, tag your traffic sources and review weekly results. Don't buy junk clicks or use forced redirects.
posts.threads: A sensible traffic test: clear landing page, relevant audience, tagged sources, weekly review. Avoid forced redirects, spam and low-quality clicks.

posts.facebook: The goal of a traffic experiment should be evidence, not a screenshot. Record where visitors came from, whether they qualified, what credits were earned and how much cash was actually credited.
posts.threads: Measure what matters: source, qualifying visits, credits, cash credited and withdrawal eligibility. Views and raw clicks alone won't tell you if a traffic program is worthwhile.
